title: Credibility assessment under ASME V&V 40 of two implicit FEA models for screw load sharing in an orthopaedic locking plate
runhead: V&V40 for plate screw load sharing
device: Orthopaedic 3.5 mm locking compression plate for diaphyseal fracture fixation

models.name: Model S — 3D solid-contact implicit FEA
models.what_it_computes: Per-screw axial and shear load fractions and plate force distribution using solid bone, plate, and screw geometries with nonlinear contact and friction

models.name: Model R — Beam–spring implicit FEA surrogate
models.what_it_computes: Per-screw axial load fractions using beam elements for plate/screws and nonlinear springs for screw–bone engagement

mechanisms.name: Four-point bending across a 10 mm diaphyseal gap
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Represents plate-dominant bending where screw axial force sharing governs construct stiffness and risk of localized screw overloading

mechanisms.name: Axial compression with 5 mm medial eccentricity
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Introduces combined compression–bending that shifts load to near-gap screws, a common worst-case clinical scenario

mechanisms.name: Pure torsion about the long-bone axis
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Produces screw group warping and differential load paths not captured by simple axial tests, relevant to twisting injuries and gait-induced torsion

deviation.detail: All factor scores are reported on a 0–7 Credibility Attainment Scale (CAS), where 0 = no evidence and 7 = comprehensive evidence sufficient for high-risk decisions.

sections: 1. Introduction: We assess two implicit finite element models intended to predict screw load sharing in a locking plate. The assessment is organized under ASME V&V 40 using only the following factors: Equivalency of input parameters, Model inputs, Numerical code verification, Numerical solver error, Test conditions, Test samples, and Use error.

2. Device and computational models: The device is a 3.5 mm locking compression plate spanning a 10 mm mid-shaft gap with locking screws in near/far cortical purchase. Model S resolves full 3D contact with friction between plate, screws, and bone surrogate; Model R represents the plate and screws with beam elements and screw–bone engagement via nonlinear axial springs.

3. Mechanisms of interest: (i) Four-point bending across a 10 mm gap, (ii) Axial compression with 5 mm medial eccentricity, (iii) Pure torsion about the long-bone axis. For each mechanism, the output of interest is the per-screw axial load fraction and plate force distribution under the specified test load.

4. Context of use and model risk rationale (risk: High): Context of use—To predict per-screw axial load fractions and plate force distribution for a new plate configuration in three standard bench-test mechanisms to support down-selection before physical testing. Rationale for High risk—The decision consequence is high (design screening that can advance or halt a construct toward verification testing), and the model influence is high (predictions directly determine which screw layouts proceed), warranting stringent credibility targets.

5. Credibility plan and scoring scale: Evidence was assembled only for the seven specified factors. Each (model × mechanism × factor) is scored on the CAS 0–7 scale. Predefined criterion for acceptability at High risk: CAS ≥ 6 for all factors across all mechanisms for at least one model; otherwise, the model is not accepted for the stated context of use.

6. Evidence acquisition—Test samples and test conditions: Test samples comprised machined polymer bone surrogates matched to 3.5 mm plate geometry; plates and screws from one manufacturing lot. Sample sizes: bending n = 6, eccentric compression n = 5, torsion n = 5. Test conditions followed standard lab protocols: (i) four-point bending with 80 mm span/40 mm load spacing, (ii) axial compression with 5 mm medial offset via spacer block, (iii) torsion with endpot rotational control at 0.5 deg/s. Environmental and fixturing details were held constant across models for parameter equivalence assessments.

7. Verification activities—Numerical code verification and numerical solver error: Code verification for each model relied on element-level benchmarks (e.g., patch/beam bending reproduction) and closed-form checks for linear subcases. Numerical solver error was quantified by mesh refinement studies, contact stabilization sensitivity, Newton–Raphson residual histories, and step-size sensitivity (static implicit).

8. Input equivalency and model inputs: Equivalency of input parameters was established by mapping bench-test loads, spans, offsets, and torque–pretension conversions to model boundary conditions and pretension loads. Model inputs included elastic moduli, Poisson’s ratios, friction coefficients, screw pretension, and spring stiffness (Model R) derived from independent measurements and supplier data. Where direct measurements were not available, literature-consistent values were adopted with stated tolerances.

9. Use error considerations: Analysts followed a standard modeling checklist with peer review; common setup pitfalls were discussed during model transfer and addressed in example templates for each mechanism.

10. Results—CAS scores for each factor by model and mechanism: Threshold for acceptance at High risk is CAS ≥ 6 for all factors. Scores (0–7) and brief evidence notes below only reference the seven permitted factors.

Model S — Four-point bending:
- Equivalency of input parameters: 6 (Span/load spacing and boundary supports matched; pretension mapped from torque with calibration.)
- Model inputs: 6 (Material/fractional friction values measured on coupons; pretension applied as bolt load.)
- Numerical code verification: 6 (Patch tests and linear beam-bending recovery matched within tolerance.)
- Numerical solver error: 5 (Converged with mild contact stabilization; mesh refinement changed per-screw loads <5%.)
- Test conditions: 6 (Four-point setup replicated; load rate and alignment consistent.)
- Test samples: 5 (n = 6; one lot; geometric tolerances documented.)
- Use error: 4 (Checklist and templates used in typical workflows.)

Model S — Eccentric axial compression:
- Equivalency of input parameters: 5 (Offset replicated via boundary conditions; minor fixture compliance not modeled.)
- Model inputs: 5 (Friction and pretension within measured ranges; sensitivity noted.)
- Numerical code verification: 6 (Same verified elements and contact formulations.)
- Numerical solver error: 4 (Contact chattering at near-gap screw; refinement reduced variability to ~8%.)
- Test conditions: 5 (Offset and axial control matched; platen stiffness approximated.)
- Test samples: 4 (n = 5; surrogate variability modest but present.)
- Use error: 4 (Analyst guidance referenced in setup notes.)

Model S — Pure torsion:
- Equivalency of input parameters: 4 (Rotational boundary matched; clamp compliance not explicitly included.)
- Model inputs: 5 (Material and friction as above; pretension retained.)
- Numerical code verification: 6 (Torsional response of shafts reproduced in linear limit.)
- Numerical solver error: 3 (Convergence difficulties at higher twist; per-screw load variation ~12% on refinement.)
- Test conditions: 5 (Twist rate and fixture geometry aligned; minimal backlash in test described.)
- Test samples: 4 (n = 5; repeatability fair.)
- Use error: 3 (General instructions provided.)

Model R — Four-point bending:
- Equivalency of input parameters: 4 (Beam end constraints approximate platen contact; spring mapping approximate.)
- Model inputs: 4 (Spring stiffness from prior calibration; limited mechanism-specific tuning.)
- Numerical code verification: 6 (Beam element checks and spring assembly tests passed.)
- Numerical solver error: 6 (Linear static steps robust; per-screw loads stable <3% on refinement.)
- Test conditions: 5 (Global spans and loads matched; local contact idealized.)
- Test samples: 5 (n = 6; single-lot components modeled.)
- Use error: 4 (Template model applied by trained analysts.)

Model R — Eccentric axial compression:
- Equivalency of input parameters: 3 (Eccentricity introduced as nodal offset; fixture compliance not representable.)
- Model inputs: 3 (Spring parameters not re-identified for combined bending–compression.)
- Numerical code verification: 6 (As above.)
- Numerical solver error: 6 (Stable solutions; mesh/step sensitivity <2%.)
- Test conditions: 5 (Offset magnitude matched; platen–construct interaction idealized.)
- Test samples: 4 (n = 5; same lot.)
- Use error: 3 (High-level instructions available.)

Model R — Pure torsion:
- Equivalency of input parameters: 2 (Warping and secondary paths not representable with axial springs alone.)
- Model inputs: 3 (No torsion-specific spring calibration.)
- Numerical code verification: 6 (Beam torsion checks acceptable.)
- Numerical solver error: 6 (Stable, linear solutions.)
- Test conditions: 5 (Twist boundary matched globally.)
- Test samples: 4 (n = 5; as above.)
- Use error: 3 (Limited procedural detail recorded.)

11. Discussion: For a High-risk context, the predefined criterion required CAS ≥ 6 for every factor in at least one model across all mechanisms. Model S met several factors in four-point bending but fell short in Numerical solver error (CAS 5) and Test samples (CAS 5), and showed more pronounced deficits in eccentric compression (Numerical solver error CAS 4; Test samples CAS 4) and torsion (Equivalency of input parameters CAS 4; Numerical solver error CAS 3; Test samples CAS 4). Model R, while robust numerically, lacked Equivalency of input parameters and Model inputs calibration for eccentric compression and torsion (CAS 2–4), preventing credible mapping of test conditions to model inputs for those mechanisms. These shortfalls directly impact the reliability of per-screw load fraction predictions under eccentric and torsional loading, which are critical to the stated context of use.

12. Conclusion: Given multiple factors below the CAS ≥ 6 threshold—specifically, insufficient Equivalency of input parameters and Model inputs for Model R in eccentric compression and torsion, and excessive Numerical solver error for Model S under torsion—the models are Not accepted for the stated context of use.
